French Grammar for Intermediate Learners: What Should You Learn After the Basics?

| Grammarist

| Writing

| Grammarist

| Writing

Grammarist

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 8:31
Instaread

Learning basic French is easy. Using it comfortably in conversations, writing clear sentences, and understanding long texts is different. Once you know common words, basic sentence structures, and a few verb tenses, you will start noticing that your progress is slowing down. You understand simple French, but forming more detailed sentences will feel difficult.

This is the stage when you need to work on intermediate French grammar.

It is also an important step if you plan to take a French proficiency exam for Canadian immigration. According to Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC), French-speaking permanent residents accounted for 8.9% of admissions outside Quebec in 2025, exceeding the government’s 8.5% target. Canada has also set a 9% target for 2026. This shows the continued importance of French language skills in Canada’s immigration plans.

So, if you already know the basics, this is a good time to improve your grammar and become more comfortable using French in real situations.

What Is French Grammar for Intermediate Learners?

French Grammar for Intermediate Learners refers to the grammar rules and sentence structures that help students move beyond basic communication. At this stage, you are not just learning how to introduce yourself or talk about your daily routine. You are learning to explain opinions, describe experiences, discuss future plans, and connect ideas.

For example, a beginner might say:

Je travaille aujourd’hui. (I am working today.)

An intermediate learner might say:

Je travaille aujourd’hui parce que je dois terminer un projet avant demain. (I am working today because I have to finish a project before tomorrow.)

The second sentence gives more information and connects two ideas. That is the kind of progress you want to make.

Let’s look at the grammar topics worth focusing on.

1. Learn French Verb Tenses Beyond the Basics

Verb tenses are one of the biggest challenges for French learners. You may already know the present tense, but intermediate communication requires you to talk about past experiences, plans, and situations that are not certain.

Here are some important tenses to practise:

Passé composé: Used to talk about completed actions in the past.

J’ai visité Paris l’année dernière. (I visited Paris last year.)

Imparfait: Used for past habits, descriptions, and ongoing situations.

Quand j’étais petit, je jouais au football. (When I was little, I used to play football.)

Futur simple: Used to discuss future events.

Je voyagerai au Canada l’année prochaine. (I will travel to Canada next year.)

Conditionnel présent: Used to express wishes, polite requests, or hypothetical situations.

Je voudrais apprendre le français. (I would like to learn French.)

Don’t try to memorise every conjugation in one sitting. Instead, practise each tense with sentences from your everyday life. Write about what you did yesterday, what you are doing today, and what you plan to do next week. This makes it easier to understand when each tense belongs in a sentence.

2. Understand French Pronouns and Their Correct Usage

Pronouns help you avoid repeating the same nouns again and again. They also make your French sound more natural.

For example:

Je regarde le film. (I am watching the movie.)

You can replace le film with le:

Je le regarde. (I am watching it.)

As you move towards intermediate French, learn how to use different types of pronouns, including:

  • Direct object pronouns: me, te, le, la, nous, vous, les.
  • Indirect object pronouns: me, te, lui, nous, vous, leur.
  • Stressed pronouns: moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles.
  • Relative pronouns: qui, que, où, dont.

Relative pronouns are particularly useful when you want to join two sentences.

For example:

J’ai un ami qui habite à Lyon. (I have a friend who lives in Lyon.)

Practise using pronouns in short conversations and written paragraphs. Once you understand their position in a sentence, your French becomes smoother and less repetitive.

3. Improve Your Understanding of French Subjunctive

The subjunctive, or subjonctif, can feel confusing at first. Unlike the indicative mood, which is generally used to express facts and certainty, the subjunctive is often used to express wishes, emotions, doubts, necessity, or uncertainty.

For example:

Il faut que tu étudies. (You need to study.)

Je suis content que tu sois ici. (I am happy that you are here.)

Notice the verb sois in the second sentence. It is a subjunctive form of être.

You will often see the subjunctive after expressions such as:

  • Il faut que (It is necessary that)
  • Je veux que (I want that)
  • Bien que (Although)
  • Je suis heureux que (I am happy that)

You don’t need to use complicated subjunctive sentences in every conversation. Start by learning common expressions and practising the verbs that follow them. This will help you recognise the structure when reading and use it more comfortably when speaking or writing.

4. Practise French Conditional Sentences

Conditional sentences help you talk about possibilities, make suggestions, and explain what you would do in a particular situation.

For example:

Si j’avais plus de temps, j’apprendrais une nouvelle langue.
(If I had more time, I would learn a new language.)

This sentence uses the imparfait in the first part and the conditionnel in the second part.

You can practise with simple situations:

  • What would you do if you lived in France?
  • Where would you travel if you had a month off?
  • What would you study if you had more time?

Try answering these questions in French. You will learn how to use conditional structures while also building your ability to express opinions and explain ideas.

5. Learn French Connectors to Join Your Ideas

Knowing grammar rules is important, but you also need to connect your sentences properly. Otherwise, your writing and speaking may sound like a list of unrelated thoughts.

French connectors help you explain reasons, show contrast, give examples, and express results.

Some useful connectors include:

  • Parce que: Because
  • Donc: So / Therefore
  • Cependant: However
  • En revanche: On the other hand
  • De plus: Furthermore
  • Par exemple: For example
  • C’est pourquoi: That is why

For example:

J’aime apprendre le français parce que cette langue m’intéresse. De plus, elle peut m’aider dans ma carrière.
(I like learning French because I am interested in the language. Moreover, it can help me in my career.)

Try using two or three connectors when writing a short paragraph. This small habit can make your answers more organised and easier to follow.

How Can Better French Grammar Help You Prepare for TCF Canada?

If you are planning to take the TCF Canada exam, intermediate grammar is an important part of your preparation. The exam assesses four language skills: listening, reading, speaking, and writing. Grammar supports all four, even though it is not tested as a separate section.

For example, understanding verb tenses and sentence structures helps you follow longer conversations and written passages. Correct pronoun usage makes your speaking more natural, while connectors help you organise your ideas in written responses.

That is why preparing for the exam involves more than memorising vocabulary or practising sample questions. You also need to understand how French works and apply those rules while communicating.

If you want guidance with this process, you can explore the TCF Canada preparation course at La Forêt French Class. A structured course can help you strengthen your French foundation, work on areas where you need improvement, and become familiar with the exam format.

The important thing is to practise all four skills instead of spending all your study time on grammar exercises alone.

How to Practise Intermediate French Grammar Every Day

You don’t need to spend several hours studying grammar every day. What matters more is regular practice.

Start by choosing one grammar topic each week. For example, spend a few days practising the passé composé and imparfait. Then move on to pronouns or conditional sentences.

Read short French articles, listen to French conversations, and notice how native speakers form their sentences. When you come across a new structure, write down an example and try making two or three sentences of your own.

You should also practise speaking aloud. Even if you make mistakes, try to use the grammar you have learned. This helps you move from simply recognising a rule to using it without thinking too much.

If you are preparing for TCF Canada, include timed speaking and writing exercises in your routine. They help you become comfortable expressing ideas within a limited time.
